answer_text:
Here are comprehensive tips to help you avoid fake job scams:

---

## 🚨 How to Avoid Fake Job Scams

### 📈 Know the Threat
Between May and late July 2025, reported job‑related scams jumped more than 1,000 percent, according to research by Newsweek and McAfee. Scammers advertise jobs the same way honest employers do — online, on job sites, social media, in newspapers, and sometimes on TV and radio — but what they want is your money and personal information.

---

### 🔍 1. Research the Company Thoroughly
Scammers often create fake job listings that appear legitimate. Always check the official employer website to see if the job is listed there. If it's not, it might be a scam. You can also look up the employer on Google and LinkedIn to make sure it's real and has actual employees.

Look up the name of the company or the person who's hiring you, plus the words "scam," "review," or "complaint" to see if others say they've been scammed by that company or person.

---

### 💸 2. Never Pay for a Job
Don't pay for the promise of a job. Honest employers, including the federal government, will never ask you to pay to get a job. Anyone who does is a scammer.

Legitimate employers do not ask for money for equipment, training, or expedited onboarding.

---

### 📧 3. Watch Out for Suspicious Communications
Be very suspicious of offers from Gmail, Yahoo, or similar personal email domains. Legitimate recruiters typically use corporate email accounts.

Scammers frequently fake emails with free web-based email accounts such as Gmail or Yahoo, and use slightly modified versions of the official employer's domain name.

Be cautious of generic emails — scammers try to cast a wide net by including little or no specific information.

---

### ⚠️ 4. Be Wary of "Too Good to Be True" Offers
If a job offer seems too good to be true — enormous salary or fantastic perks with minimal effort required — it probably is. Be cautious of unrealistic promises, as this is a common tactic used by scammers to lure people in.

Fake job postings often have vague requirements. Be cautious of opportunities that only ask for simple criteria, like being of legal age or knowing how to type. These broad qualifications may indicate that the job is not genuine.

---

### 🛑 5. Don't Share Personal Information Early
Never provide sensitive personal information (your Social Security number or bank details) early in the hiring process. Legitimate employers usually wait to ask for this information until later — typically on the first day of work.

Never provide your Tax ID number, bank details, or copies of your ID during initial conversations.

---

### 🏃 6. Don't Give In to Pressure
Take your time. Fraudulent job employers will pressure you to act quickly by paying or sharing personal information. A real employer would not pressure you to make a quick decision.

Recruiters insisting on urgency, such as "Please respond within 24 hours," could indicate a scam contact.

---

### 🔗 7. Verify Before Clicking Links or Sharing Documents
Before sharing documents or clicking links, confirm through both an official business email and a live call or video meeting scheduled from a company domain.

Avoid opening attachments from unknown senders via email, text message, or social media.

---

### 🏦 8. Never Fall for Fake Check Scams
Never bank on a "cleared" check. No honest potential employer will ever send you a check to deposit and then tell you to send on part of the money or buy gift cards with it — that's a fake check scam.

---

### 🌐 9. Use Reputable Job Platforms
Always verify the employer through independent searches and visit the company's official website to confirm the job is listed there. Stick to reputable job search websites and professional networks — they are less likely to have job scams, but they can still happen.

---

### 📣 10. Report Suspicious Listings
Save evidence — screenshots, URLs, and message histories help platforms and companies take action. Report dubious offers to the FTC to protect your data and time.

---

### 🧠 Trust Your Instincts
Ultimately, if something feels off, it probably is. Take a step back and consult someone you trust. The greater the sense of urgency and the greater the opportunity, the more likely it is a scam.
